indiaMissions/india-northeast/title: Northeast India: Khasi, Naga and Mizo Christianity
indiaMissions/india-northeast/summary: In barely a century the hill peoples of India's northeast became the most Christian region of South Asia. Welsh Calvinistic Methodists among the Khasi (from 1841), American Baptists among the Garo and the Nagas (from the 1860s–70s), and Welsh Presbyterians and British Baptists among the Mizo (from 1894) gave these peoples Roman-script literacy, schools and hospitals; but the decisive growth came through indigenous evangelists and repeated revivals in the twentieth century. By the 2011 census Christians made up about 88% of Nagaland, 87% of Mizoram and 75% of Meghalaya.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/story:
Christianity reached the northeast at the edge of British expansion into the hills between Bengal, Assam and Burma. Serampore Baptists sent the Bengali evangelist Krishna Chandra Pal to the Khasi at Sohra (Cherrapunji) in 1813, and the American Baptist missionaries Nathan Brown and Oliver Cutter, who had come from the Burma mission, settled at Sadiya in upper Assam in 1836 hoping to reach the Shan and ultimately China. These early efforts produced little, but American Baptists moved to the Brahmaputra valley (Sibsagar, Nowgong, Gauhati) and found that the hill peoples, not the Hindu Assamese, responded. The Garo converts Omed and Ramkhe were baptised at Gauhati in 1863, and Garo evangelists, not foreigners, carried the faith into the Garo Hills, where Tura became the mission centre from 1877.

The Welsh Calvinistic Methodists (later the Presbyterian Church of Wales) chose the Khasi Hills as their first foreign field. Thomas Jones arrived at Sohra on 22 June 1841, devised a Roman-script orthography for Khasi, opened schools and printed the first Khasi books; the first converts were baptised in 1846. Under later Welsh missionaries the mission spread to Shillong, Jowai and the Jaintia (Pnar) country, and the Welsh Revival of 1904–05 was echoed in a Khasi revival in 1905–06 that swept the presbyteries. Catholics, especially the Salesians of Don Bosco who arrived in Shillong in 1922, later built a Catholic community of comparable size, so that Meghalaya today is divided chiefly between Presbyterians and Catholics, with Baptists dominant among the Garo.

Among the Nagas the breakthrough came through an Assamese convert, Godhula Rufus Brown, who in 1871–72 visited the Ao village of Dekahaimong (Molungkimong); in November 1872 Edward Winter Clark baptised nine Ao men at Sibsagar. Clark and his wife Mary Mead Clark settled among the Ao at Molung in 1876, translated scripture and hymns into Ao, and the mission later moved to Impur (1894). Other American Baptists opened work among the Angami at Kohima (C. D. King from 1881, the physician Sidney Rivenburg from 1887), the Lotha at Wokha and the Sema. Growth was slow until the 1930s–50s: Christians were a small minority of Nagas at Indian independence, but conversion accelerated sharply amid the upheavals of the Second World War, the Battle of Kohima (1944) and the Naga nationalist struggle, and was reinforced by revivals in the 1950s and in 1976. The Nagaland Baptist Church Council, organised in 1937 as the Naga Hills Baptist Church Council, now claims one of the largest concentrations of Baptists anywhere.

The Mizo (Lushai) Hills were annexed by the British only in 1890–91. Two Baptists sponsored by the Arthington Aborigines Mission, J. Herbert Lorrain and Frederick W. Savidge, arrived at Aizawl on 11 January 1894, reduced Lushai to writing in the Roman alphabet (the ‘A, AW, B’ primer) and translated Luke, John and Acts before leaving in 1897. The Welsh Calvinistic Methodist David Evan Jones arrived in Aizawl in August 1897 and Edwin Rowlands in 1898, while Lorrain and Savidge returned in 1903 for the Baptist Missionary Society to the south, based at Serkawn near Lunglei. The first Mizo converts, Khuma and Khara, were baptised in 1899. A series of revivals (1906, 1913, 1919, the 1930s) reshaped Mizo culture: indigenous hymns and dance-like worship (the ‘khuang’ drum) were adopted, the bachelors' dormitory (zawlbuk) disappeared, and within half a century almost the entire population was Christian, with literacy among the highest in India.

In Manipur William Pettigrew, who arrived in Imphal in 1894, was barred by the Maharaja and the colonial political agent from working among the Hindu Meitei of the valley and moved in 1896 to Ukhrul among the Tangkhul Nagas; the Welshman Watkin Roberts founded the Thadou-Kuki Pioneer Mission (1910) among the Kuki, Hmar and related peoples. The pattern repeated across the region: Hindu or Buddhist valley and plains peoples remained largely untouched, while animist hill peoples, under the pressure of colonial administration, the end of head-hunting and village warfare, and the arrival of schools and money economy, converted in group movements. Arunachal Pradesh, closed to missionaries until well after independence, saw rapid growth from the 1970s onward, largely through Nagas, Mizos and other northeastern evangelists.

Christianity became bound up with ethnic identity and politics. Angami Zapu Phizo's Naga National Council, many of whose leaders were Baptists, declared independence in 1947 and fought the Indian state from the 1950s; the slogan ‘Nagaland for Christ’ later became a political as well as religious claim. The Mizo National Front rebellion of 1966–86 under Laldenga brought the Indian Air Force's bombing of Aizawl in March 1966 and the forced regrouping of villages; churches acted as mediators and the Presbyterian and Baptist leadership helped secure the Mizo Peace Accord of 1986. Churches have also been accused of partisanship in elections and of failing to restrain ethnic violence, as in the expulsion of Bru (Reang) people from Mizoram after 1997 and the Meitei–Kuki-Zo conflict in Manipur from May 2023, in which hundreds of churches, temples and thousands of homes were destroyed.

Today the region's churches are among the most self-supporting and missionary-minded in India. Mizo Presbyterians and Naga Baptists send hundreds of missionaries to other parts of India and to neighbouring countries, sustained by systems of tithing and ‘handful of rice’ (buhfai tham) offerings pioneered by Mizo women. The northeast thus inverted the usual Indian pattern: here Christianity is a majority, tribal, largely Protestant faith rather than a minority of Dalits and Syrian Christians.

indiaMissions/india-northeast/groupsReac: Khasi and Jaintia (Pnar) of the Khasi-Jaintia Hills, reached first by Welsh Calvinistic Methodists and later in large numbers by Catholics (Salesians from 1922).
Garo of the Garo Hills, evangelised chiefly by Garo converts of the American Baptist mission from Gauhati and Tura.
Naga peoples — Ao, Angami, Lotha, Sema (Sumi), Chakhesang, later Konyak and others — through American Baptist missions at Molung, Impur, Kohima and Wokha.
Mizo (Lushai) clans and related Hmar, Lai and Mara peoples, through Welsh Presbyterians in the north and British Baptists in the south.
Tangkhul Nagas, Kukis and other hill peoples of Manipur, through Pettigrew and the Thadou-Kuki (North East India General) Mission; the Hindu Meitei majority of the valley largely remained Hindu.
Tribal peoples of Arunachal Pradesh (Nyishi, Adi, Galo, Wancho and others), mostly after 1970 through northeastern Indian evangelists and Catholic missions.
Adivasi tea-garden labourers in Assam (Santal, Munda, Oraon), served by Catholic, Lutheran (Gossner) and Baptist churches.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/focus/0: Reducing unwritten hill languages to the Roman alphabet and translating scripture, hymns and primers.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/focus/1: Village schools, mission high schools and teacher training, which produced the region's first educated elite.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/focus/2: Training indigenous evangelists, pastors and teachers who carried the faith from village to village.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/focus/3: Medical work at stations such as Kohima, Jowai, Shillong and Durtlang (Aizawl).
indiaMissions/india-northeast/focus/4: Moral and social reform: discouraging rice beer, head-hunting, feasts of merit and traditional sacrifices.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/focus/5: Revival meetings, conventions and singing as the heart of church life.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/strategies: Comity agreements dividing the region between missions (Welsh Presbyterians in the Khasi Hills and north Mizoram, Baptists in the Garo, Naga and south Mizo hills), which produced strong single-denomination identities.
Reliance on indigenous agents from the start — Garo, Assamese, Ao and Mizo evangelists did most of the pioneering.
Roman-script literacy deliberately chosen over Bengali or Assamese script, tying literacy to the mission school and the Bible.
Early self-support: tithing, the Mizo women's ‘handful of rice’ offering and village-supported pastors.
Working under colonial protection: the Inner Line (Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873) excluded traders and settlers but admitted missionaries as agents of ‘civilisation’ in the hills.
Revival-based renewal, with indigenous hymnody and music replacing imported Welsh and American tunes in the twentieth century.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/challenges: Extreme isolation, malaria and high missionary mortality in the early decades (Sadiya, Sohra, Molung).
Head-hunting, inter-village warfare and British punitive expeditions that made missionaries part of a violent colonial frontier.
Linguistic diversity: dozens of mutually unintelligible Naga and Kuki-Chin languages each needing separate translation.
Colonial restrictions: missionaries were kept out of Manipur valley and the Naga areas beyond administered territory, and much of Arunachal was closed until late in the twentieth century.
Insurgency and counter-insurgency after 1947 (Naga and Mizo conflicts), with army operations, village regrouping and church leaders caught between rebels and the state.
Denominational splits, revivalist sects and later Pentecostal and charismatic movements dividing the older churches.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/harms/0: Missions condemned and helped dismantle institutions such as the Naga morung and Mizo zawlbuk (youth dormitories), feasts of merit, traditional festivals, songs and rice beer, causing a loss of oral heritage that churches have only recently tried to recover.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/harms/1: Close cooperation with colonial administrators — missionaries served as interpreters, recruited labour corps in the First World War and benefited from punitive pacification — tied the faith to British rule.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/harms/2: Strict comity created denominational monopolies and sometimes social pressure on dissenters; church discipline could be heavy-handed (fines, exclusion for drinking or traditional rites).
indiaMissions/india-northeast/harms/3: Christianity became fused with ethnic nationalism; churches have been accused of tolerating or legitimising insurgent violence and, later, of exclusion of non-Christian minorities such as the Bru of Mizoram.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/harms/4: In the Manipur conflict from 2023 and earlier Naga–Kuki clashes (1990s), Christian peoples fought each other along ethnic lines, exposing the limits of shared faith.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/outcomes/0: Three Christian-majority states: Nagaland (about 88% in 2011), Mizoram (about 87%) and Meghalaya (about 75%), with large Christian minorities in Manipur (41%) and Arunachal Pradesh (30%).
indiaMissions/india-northeast/outcomes/1: Roman-script literary languages (Khasi, Garo, Ao, Mizo and others) and very high literacy, with Mizoram at about 91% in 2011.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/outcomes/2: Strong, self-governing churches — the Presbyterian Church of India (Khasi-Jaintia and Mizoram synods), the Nagaland Baptist Church Council, the Baptist Church of Mizoram, the Council of Baptist Churches in Northeast India — and a large Catholic presence.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/outcomes/3: Major missionary-sending churches that support hundreds of evangelists in other Indian states and abroad.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/outcomes/4: Churches acting as civic mediators in the Naga ceasefire process and the 1986 Mizo Peace Accord.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/institutio: Presbyterian Church of India (Khasi-Jaintia Synod and Mizoram Synod), rooted in the Welsh mission.
Nagaland Baptist Church Council (1937) and the Council of Baptist Churches in Northeast India (1950).
Baptist Church of Mizoram (Serkawn) and Mizoram Presbyterian Church Synod (Aizawl).
St Edmund's College, St Anthony's College and other Catholic and Presbyterian colleges in Shillong, a regional centre of education.
Eastern Theological College, Jorhat (1905) and Aizawl Theological College.
Durtlang Presbyterian Hospital (Aizawl) and Christian hospitals at Jorhat, Shillong (Nazareth Hospital) and Kohima.
indiaMissions/india-northeast/legacy: Northeast India is the great exception in Indian Christianity: the only region where Christianity is the majority faith of whole peoples, adopted mostly in the twentieth century through indigenous evangelists, revivals and literacy rather than by colonial coercion. Its churches gave Khasi, Naga and Mizo peoples written languages and modern education, and they are now among India's most self-supporting and missionary-sending bodies, but the fusion of faith with tribal and national identity has also drawn the churches into insurgency, ethnic rivalry and the politics of the Indian frontier.
